title: Derogation and states of emergency: Article 15
subtitle: War, public emergency, and a live question in front of Parliament right now
objectives: State the Article 15 conditions for a lawful derogation and identify which rights can never be derogated from
Explain how proportionality operates in derogation cases, using Belmarsh and Brannigan and McBride as contrasting outcomes
Describe the September 2026 UK position — a proposed derogation under live parliamentary scrutiny — and explain why a lawyer must treat it as developing, not settled

leadingAuthorities.role: First Strasbourg articulation of 'war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation'
Establishes the wide margin of appreciation states receive in judging the existence of an emergency

leadingAuthorities.citation: A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56 (Belmarsh)
leadingAuthorities.role: The UK's post-9/11 derogation quashed as disproportionate and discriminatory
Strasbourg upholds a UK derogation as proportionate — the contrasting outcome to Belmarsh

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Article 15 is usually the most abstract-feeling right in the Convention — until, as now, it stops being abstract. This lesson pairs the settled doctrine with a genuinely live parliamentary process, because that combination — knowing the rule cold while reading a developing situation carefully — is exactly what a working lawyer has to do.

profileHooks.weakApplication: The doctrine here is stable; the test pool leans on applying the Article 15 conditions and the Belmarsh proportionality reasoning to new facts.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Get the four Article 15 conditions and the non-derogable rights list solid in Part 1 before the case law — the later parts assume you can recite both without hesitation.

overview.hook: Derogation is the Convention's own emergency exit — a lawful, temporary suspension of some rights when a state says the life of the nation is at stake. It has been used by the UK exactly twice in the Convention era. As this lesson is being written, a parliamentary committee is actively examining whether it is about to be used a third time.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. Treat the doctrinal core of this lesson (Lawless, Ireland v UK, Belmarsh, Brannigan and McBride) as settled law. The final part of this lesson, however, describes a genuinely breaking situation: the Joint Committee on Human Rights was, as at the date this lesson was written, conducting a live parliamentary inquiry into a UK government proposal to derogate from the ECHR under Article 15 — the first serious derogation proposal in a generation. No derogation had been made or lodged with the Council of Europe as at this date. This section is a snapshot of a developing process, not a settled outcome, and should be re-checked against current parliamentary and government sources before relying on it for anything beyond understanding how derogation works in practice.

parts.heading: What Article 15 actually permits — and what it never touches
parts.voice: briefing — states the rule precisely, the way a lawyer would need it stated before advising on live facts
body: Article 15(1) allows a state to 'take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation' — but only 'in time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation', and only where the measures are 'not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law'.

Two structural limits matter as much as the trigger itself. First, derogation is not a blank cheque: measures must be strictly required by the emergency, which imports a proportionality analysis into everything that follows. Second, Article 15(2) puts a hard floor under the whole scheme — the right to life (Article 2, save for lawful acts of war), the prohibition on torture (Article 3), the prohibition on slavery (Article 4(1)), and the prohibition on retrospective criminal punishment (Article 7) can never be derogated from, whatever the emergency.

Procedurally, Article 15(3) requires the derogating state to keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures taken and their reasons, and to notify when the measures have ceased. A derogation is also always meant to be temporary and tied to the emergency that justified it — it is not a permanent opt-out.

components.definition: A state's formal, temporary suspension of some Convention obligations during a war or public emergency threatening the life of the nation, to the extent strictly required — subject to a floor of absolutely non-derogable rights (Articles 2, 3, 4(1), 7) and a duty to notify the Council of Europe.

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order a lawyer would check them when assessing whether a proposed derogation is lawful under Article 15.
items: Is there a war or public emergency threatening the life of the nation?
Do the proposed measures touch any absolutely non-derogable right (Arts 2, 3, 4(1), 7)?
Are the measures strictly required by the exigencies of the situation?
Has the state notified the Council of Europe with reasons?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: the trigger first, then the absolute floor that can never be crossed, then proportionality of what remains, then the procedural notification duty.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the existence of an emergency is the threshold question, the non-derogable rights are an absolute floor regardless of the emergency's severity, and strict necessity is assessed only for what's left after that floor.

parts.heading: Lawless and Ireland v UK: the margin of appreciation on 'emergency'
parts.voice: structural — reference part on how much deference states get
body: Lawless v Ireland (No 3) was Strasbourg's first real engagement with Article 15, arising from Irish internment powers used against IRA activity. The Court accepted that a public emergency threatening the life of the nation existed on those facts, and in doing so set the template phrase that still governs the analysis today — an emergency involving 'an exceptional situation of crisis or emergency which affects the whole population and constitutes a threat to the organised life of the community'.

Ireland v UK, arising from internment and interrogation practices in Northern Ireland, developed this further and is equally important for what it says about the margin of appreciation: the Court held that national authorities are, in principle, better placed than an international court to judge both the existence of an emergency and the measures needed to meet it, because they have direct and continuous contact with pressing local realities.

This deference is not unlimited — it is why proportionality still bites, as Belmarsh later shows — but it means the threshold question ('is there an emergency at all?') is one on which Strasbourg gives states considerable latitude. Students often assume the hard fight in derogation cases is about whether an emergency exists; in practice, the harder fight is almost always about whether the response to it was proportionate.

components.factsShort: The UK's use of internment and the 'five techniques' of interrogation against suspected terrorists in Northern Ireland.
components.ratioShort: States are owed a wide margin of appreciation in judging the existence of a public emergency, given their direct and continuous contact with local conditions; the five techniques were, separately, found to breach Article 3.

expanded.facts: Ireland brought an inter-state case against the UK over internment without trial and interrogation practices (the 'five techniques': wall-standing, hooding, subjection to noise, sleep deprivation, and deprivation of food and drink) used against suspected paramilitaries in Northern Ireland during the Troubles.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that it fell to each state, in the first place, to determine whether the life of its nation was threatened by a public emergency, subject to European supervision; national authorities were better placed than an international judge to assess this. The five techniques, however, were found to constitute inhuman and degrading treatment contrary to Article 3 — a right from which no derogation is ever possible.
expanded.significance: Ireland v UK establishes the wide margin of appreciation on the existence of an emergency, while simultaneously demonstrating that Article 15's non-derogable floor (here, Article 3) operates completely independently of how much deference the state otherwise receives.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Ireland v UK, highlight the sentence stating the margin of appreciation ratio.
interaction.passage: The Irish Government argued the Court should assess afresh whether an emergency genuinely existed. The Court disagreed with that framing. It falls in the first place to each Contracting State, with its responsibility for the life of its nation, to determine whether that life is threatened by a public emergency, because national authorities are, by reason of their direct and continuous contact with the pressing needs of the moment, in principle better placed than an international judge to decide both on the presence of such an emergency and on the nature and scope of derogations necessary to avert it. The five techniques were nonetheless found to breach Article 3.
interaction.ratioSentence: It falls in the first place to each Contracting State, with its responsibility for the life of its nation, to determine whether that life is threatened by a public emergency, because national authorities are, by reason of their direct and continuous contact with the pressing needs of the moment, in principle better placed than an international judge to decide both on the presence of such an emergency and on the nature and scope of derogations necessary to avert it.

parts.heading: Belmarsh: when a derogation fails proportionality
parts.voice: case-narrative — the anchor case, told in full before the doctrine is extracted
body: After 9/11, the UK derogated from Article 5 (liberty) to allow indefinite detention without trial of foreign nationals suspected of terrorism, under Part 4 of the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001. Nine detainees challenged both the underlying detention and the derogation itself.

The House of Lords, by an 8–1 majority, held the derogation unlawful. Lord Bingham accepted that a public emergency could exist even without an imminent attack, giving real weight to the margin of appreciation on that threshold question — echoing Ireland v UK. But the measures failed the strict-necessity limb of Article 15(1): detention powers applied only to foreign nationals, leaving British nationals who posed an identical threat completely untouched, and detainees were free to leave the UK for any country that would take them, undermining the claim that the measure was strictly required to meet the danger.

The case is therefore not really about whether emergencies justify derogation in principle — it accepts that they can. It is about the second-stage proportionality analysis biting hard even where the first-stage deference on 'is there an emergency' is generous. A derogation that discriminates by nationality, without a rational connection between that distinction and the danger being addressed, will not survive.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say Belmarsh held there was no genuine public emergency after 9/11, and that this is why the derogation failed.
components.whyItsWrong: The House of Lords accepted the existence of a public emergency threatening the life of the nation — that finding was not overturned. The derogation failed on proportionality: the measures (detention limited to foreign nationals, with an exit option to leave the UK) were not strictly required by, or rationally connected to, the emergency they were said to address, and were also discriminatory on grounds of nationality.

interaction.prompt: Why, precisely, did the Belmarsh derogation fail?
options: Because the House of Lords found there was no genuine public emergency after all
Because the measures were not strictly required by the emergency and discriminated on grounds of nationality, without a rational connection to the danger addressed
Because the UK had not notified the Council of Europe of the derogation
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option is the most common student error — the emergency finding survived. The real ground was the disproportionality and discriminatory scope of the response, not the threshold question.

parts.heading: Brannigan and McBride: a derogation Strasbourg upheld
parts.voice: comparative — pairs against Belmarsh to sharpen the proportionality line
body: It would be easy to leave this lesson thinking derogations rarely survive scrutiny. Brannigan and McBride v UK is the necessary counterweight. It concerned a UK derogation from Article 5 permitting extended detention without judicial authorisation of terrorism suspects in Northern Ireland, made after the UK had temporarily withdrawn an earlier derogation following an adverse Strasbourg ruling in Brogan v UK.

Strasbourg upheld this derogation as valid. The emergency (ongoing terrorist violence in Northern Ireland) was not seriously disputed. On proportionality, the Court accepted that extended detention, subject to safeguards — including judicial review of the lawfulness of detention, access to a solicitor after 48 hours, and the ability to challenge detention by habeas corpus — was within the margin of appreciation the UK was entitled to, even without prior judicial authorisation of each extension.

The contrast with Belmarsh is instructive and exam-relevant: Brannigan and McBride's measures were tightly tailored, subject to real safeguards, and applied without the kind of nationality-based discrimination that sank the Belmarsh derogation two decades later. Derogation, properly used with adequate safeguards and a rational, non-discriminatory scope, is a route Strasbourg will uphold — it is loose tailoring and discriminatory reach, not derogation itself, that draws the successful challenge.

components.label: Belmarsh vs Brannigan and McBride: what made the difference
points: Both accepted the existence of a genuine public emergency — this was not the dividing line
Brannigan and McBride: measures applied to all suspects in the relevant category, without nationality discrimination
Brannigan and McBride: real procedural safeguards were built in (judicial review of lawfulness, access to a solicitor, habeas corpus)
Belmarsh: measures applied only to foreign nationals, with a rational-connection gap (British nationals posing the same risk were untouched)
Belmarsh: detainees could leave the UK entirely, undercutting the claim the measure was strictly required to meet the danger

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a derogation which is tightly tailored, non-discriminatory and subject to real procedural safeguards is more likely to survive proportionality scrutiny than one that isn't?
sliderLabels: Tailoring and safeguards make no real difference
Tailoring and safeguards are decisive to the outcome
interaction.correctPosition: Tailoring and safeguards are decisive to the outcome
interaction.explanation: The Brannigan and McBride/Belmarsh contrast is precisely this: both accepted an emergency existed, but tight tailoring and genuine safeguards (Brannigan) survived scrutiny where loosely tailored, discriminatory measures (Belmarsh) did not.

parts.heading: September 2026: live scrutiny of a proposed UK derogation
parts.voice: current-affairs briefing — explicitly provisional in tone, flagging what is known versus unresolved
body: As at the date this lesson was written, the UK has not lodged a derogation with the Council of Europe since the Article 5 derogations of the Troubles-era and post-9/11 periods discussed above — both of which, as you've now seen, ended up tested (and, in one case, defeated) in court. That makes the current situation genuinely unusual: the Joint Committee on Human Rights, the cross-party parliamentary body that scrutinises human rights compliance, was conducting a live inquiry into a government proposal to derogate from the ECHR.

A UK government proposing to derogate is rare enough on its own to be significant teaching material, independent of whatever the eventual outcome is. It puts every doctrine covered so far back into live use: does the situation said to justify derogation meet the 'war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation' threshold from Lawless and Ireland v UK? Would the specific measures proposed be strictly necessary, tightly tailored and non-discriminatory in the way Brannigan and McBride requires, or would they risk the kind of mismatch between the measure and the danger that doomed the Belmarsh derogation?

The correct approach for a law student — and for a working lawyer advising on this in real time — is not to treat this section as settled fact. No derogation had actually been lodged with the Council of Europe as at the date this lesson was written; the JCHR inquiry is a scrutiny process, not a decision. Anyone relying on this for anything beyond understanding how the doctrine would apply should check the JCHR's published reports and any government response for the current position before advising on it.

components.definition: A cross-party committee of both Houses of Parliament that scrutinises government policy and legislation for human rights compliance — its inquiries are a scrutiny and reporting function, not a legal decision, and do not themselves make or block a derogation.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this briefing extract that tells you the September 2026 situation is still developing, not a settled derogation.
interaction.scenarioText: The Joint Committee on Human Rights opened an inquiry into a government proposal that would derogate from Convention obligations. Ministers have set out the emergency said to justify it. No derogation notice has been lodged with the Council of Europe, and the Committee's report — along with any government response — was still pending as at the date this lesson was written.
tappableSpans: No derogation notice has been lodged
interaction.correctSpan: No derogation notice has been lodged
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the operative fact. Article 15(3) requires formal notification to the Council of Europe — until that happens, there is no derogation in legal effect, whatever the parliamentary and political process around it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about formal legal effect rather than political process. A JCHR inquiry, ministerial statements and a pending report are all part of scrutiny — the derogation itself only exists once notice is lodged with the Council of Europe under Article 15(3), and that had not happened.

testPool.prompt: State the Article 15(1) threshold a state must meet before it may derogate from Convention obligations.
acceptableAnswers: war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation
public emergency threatening the life of the nation
testPool.modelAnswer: A state may derogate only 'in time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation', and only to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.

testPool.prompt: Can a state ever lawfully derogate from Article 3 (prohibition on torture)?
options: No — it is absolutely non-derogable under Article 15(2)
Yes, if the emergency is severe enough

testPool.prompt: Which of these rights is NOT absolutely non-derogable under Article 15(2)?
options: Article 2 (right to life, save for lawful acts of war)
Article 3 (prohibition on torture)
Article 5 (right to liberty)
Article 7 (no punishment without law)
testPool.trapExplanation: Article 5 is exactly the right that has been derogated from in every UK example in this lesson — it is not on the Article 15(2) non-derogable list, unlike Articles 2, 3, 4(1) and 7.

testPool.prompt: What does Article 15(3) require of a state that has derogated?
options: It must keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures and reasons, and notify when they cease
It must obtain prior approval from the European Court of Human Rights before derogating
It must hold a national referendum before any derogation takes effect

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps the House of Lords used in Belmarsh to find the derogation unlawful.
items: Accept that a public emergency threatening the life of the nation existed
Note that detention powers applied only to foreign nationals
Observe that British nationals posing an identical risk were untouched by the measure
Conclude the measures were not strictly required and were discriminatory

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Belmarsh, highlight the sentence identifying the core proportionality flaw.
testPool.passage: The Secretary of State argued the derogation was a proportionate response to a genuine and serious threat. The House accepted the threat was real. However, the measures were confined to foreign nationals, leaving British nationals presenting the same threat wholly unaffected, and detainees remained free to leave the United Kingdom for any state willing to receive them. A derogation measure that leaves an equivalent domestic threat untouched, while permitting those detained simply to depart the jurisdiction, cannot be said to be strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.
testPool.ratioSentence: A derogation measure that leaves an equivalent domestic threat untouched, while permitting those detained simply to depart the jurisdiction, cannot be said to be strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.

testPool.prompt: Which derogation scenario more closely mirrors Brannigan and McBride than Belmarsh?
testPool.scenarioA: Extended detention powers applying equally to all suspects regardless of nationality, subject to judicial review of lawfulness and access to a solicitor.
testPool.scenarioB: Indefinite detention powers applying only to foreign nationals, with no equivalent measure for nationals posing the same risk, and no route to judicial review of the detention itself.
testPool.explanation: A reflects Brannigan and McBride: non-discriminatory scope plus real procedural safeguards. B mirrors the discriminatory, under-safeguarded scheme that failed in Belmarsh.

testPool.prompt: A government proposes a derogation from Article 5 in response to a cyberattack campaign it says threatens critical national infrastructure. The proposed detention powers would apply to a narrow, factually justified category of suspects regardless of nationality, with judicial oversight built in. On the doctrine in this lesson, is this measure more likely to resemble Belmarsh or Brannigan and McBride in its prospects?
options: Brannigan and McBride — tight tailoring, non-discriminatory scope and safeguards are the features that tend to survive scrutiny
Belmarsh — any derogation from Article 5 is inherently doomed to fail
Neither — Article 15 has never been tested against a non-terrorism emergency
testPool.explanation: The proportionality analysis turns on tailoring, non-discrimination and safeguards, not on the label of the emergency. Features matching Brannigan and McBride's structure point towards that outcome rather than Belmarsh's.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most strongly support an Article 14-style discrimination challenge to a proposed derogation, on Belmarsh reasoning.
testPool.scenarioText: A proposed derogation would extend detention powers. The measure is expressed to apply only to non-British nationals suspected of the relevant conduct, while British nationals suspected of identical conduct remain subject only to ordinary criminal process.
tappableSpans: British nationals suspected of identical conduct
testPool.explanation: This is the precise feature that sank the Belmarsh derogation — a nationality-based distinction with no rational connection to the risk posed, since nationals presenting an identical threat are left untouched.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Strasbourg gives states a wide margin of appreciation specifically on the question of whether a public emergency exists at all (as opposed to whether the response to it is proportionate)?
sliderLabels: No real deference on either question
Wide deference on the existence of an emergency; proportionality is scrutinised more closely
testPool.correctPosition: Wide deference on the existence of an emergency; proportionality is scrutinised more closely
testPool.explanation: Ireland v UK sets a wide margin on the threshold 'emergency' question; Belmarsh then shows the proportionality stage is where derogations are actually won or lost.

testPool.prompt: A government derogates from Article 5 during a declared national emergency, introducing detention powers that apply to all suspects regardless of nationality, but with no judicial review mechanism at all and no maximum detention period specified. Analyse whether this derogation is likely to be proportionate.
factsToOrder: A national emergency has been declared and is not seriously disputed
The measure applies without nationality discrimination
There is no judicial review mechanism
No maximum detention period is specified

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the derogation is 'strictly required by the exigencies of the situation' under Article 15(1).
modelAnswer.rule: A derogation must be strictly necessary and proportionate; tailoring, non-discrimination and procedural safeguards are central to that assessment (Brannigan and McBride; Belmarsh, by contrast, on discriminatory and under-safeguarded measures).
modelAnswer.application: The non-discriminatory scope is a point in the measure's favour, consistent with Brannigan and McBride. However, the total absence of judicial review and of any maximum detention period is a significant departure from the safeguards Strasbourg accepted as adequate in Brannigan and McBride, where judicial review of lawfulness and access to a solicitor were built in.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The lack of judicial oversight and of a defined maximum detention period makes this derogation vulnerable to a finding of disproportionality, notwithstanding its non-discriminatory scope.

testPool.prompt: As at September 2026, had a UK derogation from the ECHR actually been lodged with the Council of Europe?
options: No — a parliamentary inquiry into a proposal was underway, but no derogation notice had been lodged
Yes — a derogation was already in force

testPool.prompt: What is the legal effect of a Joint Committee on Human Rights inquiry into a proposed derogation, on its own?
options: It is a scrutiny and reporting function of Parliament; it does not itself create or block a derogation
It automatically triggers a derogation once the inquiry opens
It gives the Committee a veto that legally prevents the government from derogating
testPool.trapExplanation: Both wrong answers overstate the Committee's legal power. A derogation only takes legal effect once formally lodged with the Council of Europe under Article 15(3) — parliamentary scrutiny is a political and reporting process running alongside that, not a substitute for it.

testPool.prompt: A student is asked, in September 2026, to advise on 'the UK's current Article 15 derogation'. What is the most accurate first step in the answer?
options: Describe the Belmarsh derogation as though it remains current, since it is the leading case
Note that, as at the relevant date, no derogation notice had been lodged with the Council of Europe — the correct framing is a live proposal under parliamentary scrutiny, not an existing derogation
Refuse to answer, since Article 15 cannot be discussed while any inquiry is ongoing
testPool.explanation: Precision about legal status matters here: describing an unresolved parliamentary scrutiny process as though it were an existing derogation would misstate the law as it actually stood.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson is treating 'was there an emergency?' as the decisive battleground. In practice — Ireland v UK, Belmarsh and Brannigan and McBride all show this — that question gets wide deference; the real fight, and the one worth spending exam time on, is proportionality: tailoring, discrimination, and safeguards.
